title: Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year
description: Singer-songwriter and Variety Hitmakers 2024 honoree Raye has won the 2026 Mercury prize for her epic second studio album, “This Music May Contain
body:
Singer-songwriter and Variety Hitmakers 2024 honoree Raye has won the 2026 Mercury prize for her epic second studio album, “This Music May Contain Hope,” beating out Olivia Dean, Paul McCartney and others for the prize.

	The Mercury Prize has no real equivalent in the U.S., and is intended to recognize music from the U.K. and Ireland; the Brit Awards are more of a British equivalent to the Grammys. Past Mercury Prize best album winners include Arlo Parks, Little Simz, the XX, James Blake and others.
	

	Raye’s album topped fellow nominees Dave (for “The Boy Who Played the Harp”), Dove Ellis (“Blizzard”). Florence + the Machine (“Everybody Scream”), Jade (“That’s Showbiz Baby!”), Knats (“A Great Day in Newcastle”), Kojey Radical (“Don’t Look Down”), Nia Archives (“Emotional Junglist”), Olivia Dean (“The Art of Loving”), Paul McCartney (“The Boys of Dungeon Lane”), Suede (“Antidepressants”) and the War Child “Help(2)” compilation.


	Variety wrote of Raye’s album: “Suffice it to say, the album does not lack for ambition: Divided into four sections based on the seasons, it sprawls across a surprisingly fast-moving 70 minutes, 17 songs and nearly as many styles. Inevitably, it runs the risk of being too much for some listeners: too many songs, too many stylistic pivots, too much of… well, basically everything. This is not an album for background listening — it basically demands your attention.

	“But as artists from Queen to Beyoncé have proven, ambition and excess can be glorious things when deployed with intelligence and humor, and while we’re not equating Raye with either of the above, there’s a similar sense here of trusting the artist to take you on an interesting voyage without wasting your time.”
	

	Performers at the show included Suede, Pulp, and others.

schema.headline: Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year

title: John Mayer Sets Up His Own Label, Sob Rock Records, in Partnership With Mercury to Release First New Solo Music in Five Years
description: John Mayer has had his hands full with what felt like a hundred projects over the past few years — with putting out new music not among them. It ta
body:
John Mayer has had his hands full with what felt like a hundred projects over the past few years — with putting out new music not among them. It takes a stretch of the memory to even recall that he announced a parting of ways with Sony Music back in 2022, with no followup revelation about where, if anywhere, he planned to go next . Now, after hinting at the beginning of this year that new studio recordings were afoot, he’s finally publicly kicking the recording artist part of his career back into gear.
	

	Mayer and associates announced Thursday that he has started up his own label, Sob Rock Records — which shares the name of the last album he put out for Sony, 2021’s “Sob Rock” — to be operated in partnership with Universal Music’s Mercury Records. No album has yet been announced, but his first single in five years, “Tom and Jerry,” is arriving under his new shingle Friday.


	“Working with Tyler Arnold and the talented team at Mercury Records has already proven to be a great partnership,” Mayer said in a statement. “The path from creative vision to execution has never been easier or more rewarding. I feel very inspired, and I’m excited for what’s to come.”

	“John Mayer is one of the greatest artists of all time,” said Arnold, Mercury’s chairman-CEO, and I couldn’t be prouder to welcome him to Mercury Records. We’re excited to be part of his next chapter and to partner with his label, Sob Rock Records, to help bring his creative vision to life.”

	The new single arrives at DSPs at the usual midnight hour as Thursday turns into Friday, but listeners to the artist’s SiriusXM channel, Life With John Mayer, will get a preview throughout the day Thursday. The song was produced by Blake Slatkin with Mayer and mixed by Serban Genhea.
	

	It almost goes without saying that the credits acknowledge the song was recorded at Chaplin Studios. One of Mayer’s biggest endeavors in the past couple of years was joining forces with the film director McG to purchase the Hollywood lot that started as Charlie Chaplin’s studio and eventually became the home of A&M, then Henson Studios. Mayer and McG shared their experience with taking the reins of the studio with Variety at the top of 2026; read about that here. 

	The singer-songwriter-guitarist indicated then that 2026 would mark a turn back toward his solo recording career after several years of focusing on his role as co-frontman of Dead & Company, including being the primary designer of both of that group’s residencies at Sphere in 2024 and 2025.

	Mayer was already known to be coming back as a live performing artist in a big way with a run of shows booked for Sphere in Las Vegas next year. He currently has concerts at the venue booked for April 8 through June 12, all of them in a configuration that will see him doing separate sets with his full band, with the John Mayer Trio and as a solo performer.

schema.headline: John Mayer Sets Up His Own Label, Sob Rock Records, in Partnership With Mercury to Release First New Solo Music in Five Years

title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on AI: ‘An Amazing Piece of Technology’ But ‘I’m Not Embracing It at All’
description:
“Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI.

	“I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI F
body:
“Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI.

	“I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI Fest’s opening night U.S. premiere of “Wildwood.” “I see technology as a tool, and we use technology at Laika. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is a computer is technology. Technology is useful when you put it in the hands of people, when you put it in the hands of artists who can amplify their voice.
	

	“Technology is not useful when it takes the place of the artist, and that’s the concern with generative AI,” he continued. “It’s an amazing piece of technology, but the concern is that when it supplants the artist, then we have an issue because the computer cannot speak about humanity at all. It doesn’t know what it feels like.”


	“Wildwood” is a stop-motion fantasy feature about a young girl (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) who travels into a forbidden forest when her baby brother is kidnapped by a murder of crows. It took 16 years to complete the film, Knight said.

	“Sixteen years is a long time,” Knight said. “As I’ve said before, this film is old enough to have driven me to the premiere tonight. But it’s a funny thing because it’s a big fantasy story. It’s a big sweeping adventure story. It’s a beautiful extravaganza. It’s an epic, but that’s not something that sustains you for 16 years.

	He continued, “At the heart of it, it has to be something that means something to you and that’s the thing I’m most proud of is that underneath it all, it is something that is really heartfelt, it’s beautiful, it’s emotional and that’s the thing I hope audiences take away from this.”
	

	Knight doesn’t believe that AI could have helped speed up the process — at least not if he wanted to maintain the highest quality. “That very notion fills me with rage,” he said. “Look, that’s the world we live in and the technology seems like it’s only pushing us in one direction, which is everything is going to be simpler. Everything is going to be automated; everything is going to be easier. What I would say to that is that there is something special about the human touch. There is something beautiful about humanity. And that’s one thing that stop motion represents. Stop-motion represents humanity at its finest creativity, emotion, care, devotion, time.

	“That’s something that AI could never do because a computer has never felt anything,” Knight added. “It’s never felt loss or love or pain, and that’s something that people can feel and that’s something you feel in something that was made by people.”



	

					“Wildwood”
									Courtesy of Laika
	



	The cast of “Wildwood” also includes Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Jake Johnson, Carey Mulligan, Maya Erskine, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg and Tantoo Cardinal.

	Bassett talked about recording her work during COVID. “I wanted to get out of the house, get creative again,” she told me. “It was just right on time.”


	See photos from the AFI Fest premiere of “Wildwood” below.

title: ‘Line of Fire’ Gets Full 18-Episode Season Order at NBC
description:
“Line of Fire” has been given a full 18-episode season order at NBC.

	The freshman action thriller series is one of the fall season’s breakout hit
body:
“Line of Fire” has been given a full 18-episode season order at NBC.

	The freshman action thriller series is one of the fall season’s breakout hits, with NBC’s best delayed-viewing lift in more than three years.

	Initially slated for 13 episodes, NBC gave a back order to five additional scripts with the hope of extending the season as a result of sustained viewership. Now, the first season is officially getting 18 total episodes and will extend into 2027.
	

	“Line of Fire” follows a family of agents from various branches of federal law enforcement who find themselves tangled in a deadly conspiracy. They bridge personal differences and cross professional boundaries “as they tackle cases for the FBI, US Marshals, Secret Service and Department of Justice,” per the logline. “After a seemingly cut-and-dry case turns into a deadly conspiracy, they must use the expertise from a lifetime of protecting civilians and politicians to protect one another and bring the killer to justice … even if it means betraying their sworn code.”


	Peter Krause stars in the series alongside Hope Davis, Kat Cunning, Tommy O’Brien, Taylor Bloom and Charlie Barnett. Creator and writer Joshua Safran executive produces with Jenna Bush Hager and Ben Spector. The series is produced by Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.

	“Line of Fire” airs on Mondays at 10 p.m. and streams the next day on Peacock.

	Variety TV critic Aramide Tinubu praised the show in her review, saying it “has all the makings of becoming a classic in the canon of beloved police procedurals.”

schema.headline: ‘Line of Fire’ Gets Full 18-Episode Season Order at NBC

title: The ‘Terrifier’ Trilogy Is Returning to Theaters for a Halloween Run
description:
Art the Clown is back for another round of big-screen terror.

	The “Terrifier” trilogy is headed back to theaters, just in time for spooky season.
body:
Art the Clown is back for another round of big-screen terror.

	The “Terrifier” trilogy is headed back to theaters, just in time for spooky season. 2016’s “Terrifier,” 2022’s “Terrifier 2″ and 2024’s “Terrifier 3″ will have showtimes at Regal theaters nationwide on Halloween weekend, from Oct. 29-31. The re-release is presented by the video game “Dead by Daylight” and Behaviour Interactive, with support from distributors Cineverse and Epic Pictures.
	

	Ticketholders for any of the films will be entered into a drawing to win a download code for “Dead by Daylight,” which features “Terrifier” anti-hero Art the Clown as a character. All Regal Crown Club members who buy tickets will receive a code for an in-game cosmetic — in this case, Art’s retro flower sunglasses.


	The gory, low-budget “Terrifier” movies became surprise box office sensations with the second and third chapters. “Terrifier 2″ made $16.8 million worldwide from a $250,000 budget and “Terrifier 3″ wowed with over $90 million worldwide from a $2 million budget.

	Damien Leone wrote and directed the trilogy, which stars David Howard Thornton as Art the Clown. Lauren LaVera plays Sienna Shaw, the series’ protagonist, who joins in the second chapter. 

	In an interview with Variety when the third film was released, Leone discussed how he pushed things to the limit in his films. 

	“I’m always looking for lines to get up to, to push the boundary,” he said. “Maybe just step right over it. But you can absolutely fall into a level of extreme distaste that I’m trying not to do.”
	

	Watch the trailer for the first “Terrifier” below.

schema.headline: The ‘Terrifier’ Trilogy Is Returning to Theaters for a Halloween Run

title: Ellen Burstyn on Going for the EGOT With Her Favorite Poems and Being Over ‘The Exorcist’: ‘It’s Enough Already’
description:
I asked Ellen Burstyn where a Grammy would go, if she ever won one. She stands up to show me.

	“I wonder if I took my iPad off the stand and walke
body:
I asked Ellen Burstyn where a Grammy would go, if she ever won one. She stands up to show me.

	“I wonder if I took my iPad off the stand and walked you into my office, where they all are,” she says, immediately reaching for it over a video Zoom. Her assistant, Caitlin, gets the camera turned around, and the Zoom window swings from a living room into a study. Burstyn, 93, narrates as she goes, approaching the wall of statues.


	“There’s the Emmy, the Tony, the Golden Lion, the Oscar and the other Emmy,” she tells Variety sweetly. “And then these are all awards, too, from various organizations and people. And then these are my nominations up there,” pointing to dozens of certificates and plaques.
	

	I tell her the good news is that the Grammy is smaller than most of those, so it won’t take up as much room.

	“Yeah, it’ll fit,” she says wryly. Then, during the walk back: “That’s the first time I’ve ever shown that to anybody. Nobody asked before.”

	That shelf is the reason we’re talking.

	Burstyn won her Oscar for “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore” and her Tony for “Same Time, Next Year” in the same year, 1975. Her two Emmys came decades later, for “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” (2009) and “Political Animals” (2013). This past September she accepted the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Film Festival, presented at the screening of Maggie Gyllenhaal’s short “Flesh Impact,” in which she plays Marilyn Monroe.

	This leaves one letter in the entertainment gold standard.

	“Poetry Says It Better: Poems to Help You Wake Up,” published in April by HarperCollins, is Burstyn’s personal collection of the poems that have carried her through nearly nine decades, from Edna St. Vincent Millay to Mary Oliver to Rumi, whose birthplace she once made a pilgrimage to see. She read the audiobook herself — five hours and nine minutes of it — and it earned a Kirkus Star and an Earphones Award. It is now a contender for the Grammy for best audiobook, narration and storytelling recording. If she wins, Burstyn, who turns 94 in December, would complete her EGOT and become the oldest person ever to do it, passing John Gielgud, who was 87. She would be the seventh woman, after Helen Hayes, Rita Moreno, Audrey Hepburn, Whoopi Goldberg, Jennifer Hudson and Viola Davis.
	

	Burstyn hadn’t been thinking about any of that. But her granddaughter had.

	“She said, ‘You know, you’re only one away from an EGOT. You should go for it, Grandma,'” Burstyn recalls. “I don’t know how you ‘go for it.’ But it is thrilling. I understand only six women have ever gotten an EGOT. That’s quite a special event, so I’m all for it.”

	We last spoke in 2020 during the pandemic, also over Zoom, when the Netflix drama “Pieces of a Woman” put her in the conversation to become the oldest supporting actress nominee in Oscar history. She told me then that she loved breaking records as she got older. And even though she missed out on a nom, she hasn’t changed her position.

	What she wanted to talk today about was the poetry. Asked what she loves about these poems, she didn’t explain, but instead recited William Ernest Henley’s “Invictus” — the poem that hit her in high school — while looking directly at the camera, start to finish, from memory.

	“I read that, and I was just so reassured somehow that the stuff I was going through in my life at the time wasn’t going to be forever,” Burstyn says. “That went into my heart, and gave me such confidence that my life was going to change. That started my life as a poetry lover.”

	Burstyn has never been nervous acting, she says. Her first Broadway audition — in 1957, for a two-act comedy called “Fair Game” — got her the lead. What changed her was realizing that natural ability wasn’t enough, leaving Hollywood for New York and studying with Lee Strasberg. She is now co-president of the Actors Studio, and her advice to young actors is the same thing she learned there: “A creative act comes from the heart.”

	When I ask whether she looks at that shelf with pride, her answer is surprising.

	“I could have done better. There are things I didn’t do that I should have done, and things that Lee Strasberg encouraged me to do that I wish I had done. So I don’t feel like a success. Yes, I won awards, and yes, I’ve enjoyed my work. I like to work. But I wish I had gone into the great plays of the theater and played those more. I’m disappointed that I didn’t do that.”

	Everything happens for a reason, I tell her. And it’s usually our jobs, the cinephiles and admirers of art, to proclaim to the world what her work has meant, and how important it’s been.
	

	As for the new “Exorcist” film — Mike Flanagan’s “The Exorcist: Martyrs,” with Scarlett Johansson — coming next year, more than 53 years after Burstyn’s Chris MacNeil was at the center of that sensation, she expresses dismay. “Isn’t there enough already of the ‘Exorcist’ thing?” she exclaims. “It’s enough already.”

	Burstyn has a closing argument for the Recording Academy. “I really enjoy reciting poetry and reading it, and I hope people will read the book,” she says. “But I also hope they will listen to the recording that comes with the book — because I think poetry should be heard.”

schema.headline: Ellen Burstyn on Going for the EGOT With Her Favorite Poems and Being Over ‘The Exorcist’: ‘It’s Enough Already’

title: Laika’s First PG-13 Film, Brad Bird’s Neo-Noir and an Alzheimer’s Memoir: Animation’s Revolution Isn’t for Kids
description: The MPA gave “Wildwood” a PG-13 for “strong fantasy violence/bloody images, thematic material, suicide-related material, brief partial nudity and l
body:
The MPA gave “Wildwood” a PG-13 for “strong fantasy violence/bloody images, thematic material, suicide-related material, brief partial nudity and language,” which is a mouthful for any movie and an especially wild one for a stop-motion picture about a girl hunting for her kidnapped baby brother.

	It’s the first PG-13 in Laika’s 17 years as a feature studio, and at 130 minutes, it ties the record for the longest English-language animated film ever made. Travis Knight, who runs the Portland, Ore., studio and directed “Wildwood,” didn’t land there by accident. Anyone who remembers how dark the back half of “Kubo and the Two Strings” got probably isn’t shocked he went this far.
	

	Knight is one of the filmmakers taking part in this year’s Pixels and Pencils panel, Variety’s animation directors conversation at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, now in its fifth year. Joining Knight at the event are Brad Bird (“Ray Gunn”), Daniel Chong (“Hoppers”), Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado (“Forgotten Island”) and Leah Nelson (“Tangles”).


	The SCAD Savannah Film Festival runs Oct. 24-31.

	The panel has turned into a decent crystal ball leading to the Academy Awards. The director of “Flow,” Gints Zilbalodis, participated in 2024 before the little indie feature that could upset the big studios for the animated feature Oscar and last year, four of the eventual five nominees at the 98th Academy Awards, including winner “KPop Demon Hunters,” spoke at the event.

	Since “Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio” won the animated feature Oscar the 95th ceremony, the trophy hasn’t gone back to Disney or Pixar (“The Boy and the Heron,” “Flow” and “KPop” followed), which is a real shift for a category those two studios have owned since “Shrek” took the first trophy in the category in 2002.
	

	But this year, animation’s auteurs are making the movies they want to make.



	

					RAY GUNN — Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) and Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson).
									‘Ray Gunn’ ©2026 Skydance Animation
	



	Bird’s “Ray Gunn” is the easiest place to start, partly because the man has been chasing it since 1996, when a B-52s song and a Henry Mancini tune got tangled in his head and spit out a title. That was three years before “The Iron Giant” bombed at the box office (still a masterpiece, by the way) and then spent the next 25 years becoming the movie an entire generation of dads can’t get through without tearing up.

	He’s pitched his new film as “The Maltese Falcon” meets “Buck Rogers.” Sam Rockwell is Raymond Gunn, a gumshoe working a murder in Metropia, a version of 1939 that never happened, where humans and aliens share the same smoky streets. Netflix will release it Dec. 18, after London Film Festival screenings and a limited 70mm run. The PG rating comes with a note about “suggestive material,” which, if you know Bird’s work, tracks. Indeed, the Pixar licensing cash cow and family-friendly adventure “The Incredibles” was about a guy who hates his insurance job and misses his glory days.

	Chong’s “Hoppers” is the on the list our nieces and nephews have already watched twice on Disney+. The Pixar original opened to $46 million in March, the best start for an original since “Coco” in 2017 and cleared $500 million worldwide in about five weeks, which felt like the whole studio exhaling after “Elemental” and “Elio” stumbled out of the gate. Chong, who created “We Bare Bears” for Cartoon Network, made his feature directing debut with the story of Mabel (Piper Curda), a college student who uploads her mind into a robot beaver so she can talk to animals and keep developers from bulldozing their forest.

	It’s a family movie, sure. It’s also about habitat loss and how much people are willing to give up to stop it, and there’s a robot face removal scene that has reportedly sent some of the younger audience members out to the lobby. Timely, no?

	Crawford was on our very first panel back in 2022 with “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” the Oscar-nominated sequel nobody asked for that turned out to be a pretty frank movie about a cat who’s afraid to die. And people loved it. Mercado, his best friend in real life, co-directed that one too and their friendship, which goes back to “Kung Fu Panda 2,” is the seed of “Forgotten Island.”
	

	In the film, Jo (H.E.R.) and Raissa (Liza Soberano) grew up together in the Philippines in the 1990s and are about to be pulled apart, with Raissa off to Caltech and Jo staying home. Then they get stuck in Nakali, a place out of Philippine folklore that eats memories and if they don’t find a way out, they’ll forget each other entirely. You don’t need to have been 18 years old in Manila in the 1990s to feel that one. So seeing DreamWorks throw this kind of muscle behind a Filipino story with universal appeal means something.

	As for Laika, the studio is five for five in animated feature nominations, from “Coraline” to “Missing Link” and zero for five in wins, although “Missing Link” beat “Toy Story 4” and “Frozen II” at the Golden Globes.Knight, who got his own nomination for “Kubo,” directs the Chris Butler adaptation of Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis’ 2011 novel. In the stop-motion feature, Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) goes into the forbidden woods outside Portland after her brother is taken and stumbles into a war. The Laika crew built 136 sets and 231 puppets to get her there. Fathom releases “Wildwood” on Oct. 23, the day before Savannah kicks off.



	

									IFC
	



	Then there’s “Tangles,” which isn’t pretending to be anything other than a movie for adults. Nelson, a first-time feature director, wrote it with Sarah Leavitt, adapting Leavitt’s graphic memoir about her mother’s Alzheimer’s in the late 1990s. Abbi Jacobson voices Sarah, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus plays her mom and is among the producers with Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen.

	It got a seven-minute ovation at Cannes before Independent Film Company picked it up, and the charcoal-heavy animation does something with memory that live action could not pull off. The jokes are there early but the tears come fast and furious by credits roll.

	Both “Tangles” and “Wildwood” are also going drama at the Golden Globes, where animated titles have usually defaulted to comedy. It’s category paperwork, technically, but it says a lot about how these teams want their films seen.

	None of this is exactly new, by the way. “Persepolis” and “Anomalisa” were nominated by the Oscars years ago, and Japanese studios have been making animation for grown-ups for as long as we’ve been watching movies. Only three animated films, “Beauty and the Beast,” “Up” and “Toy Story 3,” have ever been nominated for best picture and the last of those was 15 years ago. What feels different in 2026 is the confidence. Nobody on this panel seems to be asking whether their story is “allowed” to be animated.
	

	They grew up on Saturday morning cartoons. Now they’re making them for Saturday night.

title: Chaka Khan to Be Honored at Soul Train Awards (TV News Roundup)
description:
Chaka Khan will receive the Classic Soul Honor at the 2026 Soul Train Awards, celebrating the singer-songwriter’s influence on R&B.

	Across her ca
body:
Chaka Khan will receive the Classic Soul Honor at the 2026 Soul Train Awards, celebrating the singer-songwriter’s influence on R&B.

	Across her career, which spans more than five decades, Khan helped shape the sound of soul, funk and R&B with her music, including hits like “Tell Me Something Good,” “Sweet Thing,” “Ain’t Nobody,” “I’m Every Woman” and “I Feel for You.” She received 11 Grammys, including the Recording Academy’s Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award, and was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2023 with the Musical Excellence Award.
	

	“Chaka Khan is the embodiment of soul music,” said Louis Carr, the president of BET. “From her groundbreaking work with Rufus to a solo career that has produced some of the most iconic records in music history, she has continually expanded the possibilities of R&B and soul while inspiring generations of artists to find and own their voices. Honoring Chaka is a celebration of the music and cultural legacy that Soul Train has always embodied.”


	Airing Nov. 27 on BET and CBS, the Soul Train Awards are executive produced by Jesse Collins. Dionne Harmon and Jeannae Rouzan-Clay also serve as executive producers, with Jesse Collins Entertainment as the production company for the show. Connie Orlando is the exec producer for BET. 

	In other TV roundup news:
	
		First Looks/Trailers	

	National Geographic revealed the trailer for “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” which premieres Nov. 13.

	Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho (“Moana”), the one-hour special showcases the National Geographic and Rolex Perpetual Planet Ocean Expeditions documenting the impact of rapid environmental change on all five ocean basins. The documentary follows teams of National Geographic explorers investigating the ocean. 
	

	In the Southern Ocean, three new discoveries surface, including the first-known live sighting of a giant Antarctic gonate squid. Two teams work to understand the impact of rising temperatures on Pacific Ocean ecosystems. The first deep-sea scientist from the Seychelles dives below the surface of the Indian Ocean. Local students train to measure the Atlantic Ocean’s depth along the Gambian coastline. A team works to study the Arctic Ocean, warming at four times the rate of the rest of the planet.

	The documentary is presented by the National Geographic Society in partnership with Rolex and produced by Offspring Films. Katharine Arthy is director. Executive producers include Sam Hodgson for Offspring Films, Vanessa Serrao and Kaitlin Yarnall for National Geographic Society and Tracy Rudolph Jackson for National Geographic.

	“Expedition: Saving Our Seas” premieres Nov. 13 at 9 p.m. EST on National Geographic and will stream the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

	Watch the trailer below.


	
		Programming	

	Five bonus episodes of “Lot Patrol,” from Manny Halley Productions, will debut on BET on Nov. 3.

	“Lot Patrol” looks at Hollywood through the lens of an eccentric group of security guards as they patrol a major studio backlot. The comedy series will round out its first season at 10 full episodes after the special premiere.

	The series features DeRay Davis (“21 Jump Street,” “Semi-Pro”), Carl Anthony Payne II (“Martin,” “House Party”), Tamera Kissen (“White Men Can’t Jump,” “House Party”) and comedians Skeet Carter, TK Kirkland, Alex Thomas, Tanjareen Thomas, Lionell Dalton, Nick Nervies, Dawn Raven, Iyana Halley and G Thang.

	“’Lot Patrol’ is a fresh, culturally rooted take on the industry. People inside and outside entertainment are realizing that the business of Hollywood is actually quite comical through a certain lens,” creator Manny Halley said. “It’s OK to laugh at how things in this town operate — particularly through an urban lens, which is a fresh angle. With this unbelievable ensemble of comedic talent, audiences get exactly what they’re looking for: a unique, genuine tone that is refreshingly different.”

	“Lot Patrol” is produced by Manny Halley Productions, a division of Imani Media Group. The series is created and written by Halley and Ernest L. Dancy. Manny Halley Jr., Maureen Pierre and DeRay Davis are producers. Erik White is director.
	



	*

	“The Biggest Little Farm Series,” a 12-part docuseries and sequel to the documentary “The Biggest Little Farm,” premieres Nov. 8 on YouTube.

	The original film follows John and Molly Chester and their team as they transform a depleted farm into a thriving ecosystem. Eight years later, their experiment has become far more wild than they had ever imagined. The series will “dive deeper into the lives of the creatures. It will shed light on the battle between predator and prey, farmer and pest, and reminds audiences that Nature has its own way. To balance the chaos, there’s one question the stewards cannot escape: Can a farm become too feral for its own good?”

	“The Biggest Little Farm Series” is presented by the Artemis Rising Foundation. It is directed by John Chester and is produced by Tom Quinn, Paul Gurinas, Jessica Gurinas and Shannon Green. John Chester, Erica Messer, Regina K. Scully and Sandra Keats are executive producers while Amy Overbeck and Ali Galante are co-executive producers.

	Watch the full trailer here:



	*

	Hearst Media Production Group has announced a second season of “Home for Good.” The series will return to ABC stations nationwide on Saturday, Jan. 9 as part of the “Weekend Adventure” educational informational programming block.

	Hosted by Art Edmonds, “Home for Good” is a “home renovation series honoring people who make a difference in their communities. Each half-hour episode transforms a room or personal space to better serve people who dedicate their lives to helping others. Season 2 will continue to feature first responders while bringing more community champions and service workers into the spotlight, including educators, mentors and volunteers who serve families in need.”

	“We’re excited to bring Home for Good back for a second season,” Bryan Curb, president of HMPG, said. “The series shows what giving back looks like through the people who serve their communities, while giving viewers practical fire and CO safety information they can use at home. That combination reflects the value of E/I programming: stories that educate, inform and offer a meaningful benefit to audiences.”
	
	
		Specials	

	“The Pursuit: F1 Academy” documentary special will premiere Nov. 19 on Disney+.

	The special follows F1 Academy, the all-female racing series created by Formula 1 to prepare young women for higher levels of motorsport. Fans will get behind-the-scenes access to the 2025 Academy season, following a group of elite drivers including Doriane Pin, Maya Weug, Chloe Chambers and Alisha Palmowski.

	“The Pursuit: F1 Academy” was filmed across global locations during the 2025 racing season and will also provide insight into the teams and leadership shaping F1 Academy, including managing director Susie Wolff.

	The documentary special was produced in association with ESPN as the latest extension of the “Fuel the Magic” partnership between Disney, Formula 1 and F1 Academy. The collaboration was first launched at the Formula 1 Chinese Grand Prix 2026 and expanded to the Grand Prix Du Canada 2026 to include the Academy with classic Disney icons Minnie Mouse and Daisy Duck.

	“The Pursuit: F1 Academy” will air ahead of the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix 2026 on Nov. 19-21. The special will also be available to stream on the ESPN app later this year.

title: Music Industry Moves: Liz Morentin Launches Greenvalley Media & Marketing
description: Veteran communications exec Liz Morentin has launched Greenvalley Media & Marketing, focusing on entertainment, media and technology companies and
body:
Veteran communications exec Liz Morentin has launched Greenvalley Media & Marketing, focusing on entertainment, media and technology companies and their leaders.

	Morentin most recently served as SVP and head of global communications and brand strategy at Virgin Music Group, and over the years has held top roles at Warner Bros. Records, Paradigm Talent Agency, Live Nation, RCA Records, and Dick Clark Productions.


	“Our industry has transformed so much over the years making it possible for so many more businesses and executives to achieve global success and become highly regarded global industry players, from indie record labels and distributors to tech platforms and media companies. I’m launching Greenvalley to support these businesses and executives looking to build their reputation, grow their business, and reach the right audiences,” said Morentin.
	

	+ Three Six Zero have announced a new division, Entertainment & New Media spearheaded by Rebecca Dowell. According to the announcement, Dowell, who joined Three Six Zero in 2024, will lead a strategic focus on talent across the entertainment and digital media landscape. She will be seeking dynamic, boundary-pushing talent including digital creators, multi-hyphenate creatives and IP based projects that are shaping culture across platforms and redefining how audiences engage with content.

	Her roster includes Amelia Dimoldenberg, whose “Chicken Shop Date” recently secured a licensing deal for distribution on Netflix, as well as British Comedy Award winner and BAFTA-nominated comedian, actor and satirist Munya Chawawa.
	

	Dowell previously served as talent director at YMU Group and head of talent for management company Moxie, at Studio71UK.

	+ Veteran singer-guitarist and founding Runaways guitarist/singer Lita Ford has signed with Frontiers Music Srl and will debut her new single, “Dracula,” on October 27, with an album to follow.

	“It’s been a long journey to create this magical dark fairytale album for everyone to enjoy” Ford said. “I needed the perfect team to make that happen and to help give this powerful record a life it deserves. I am so happy to say I have officially sealed the deal with Frontiers Music Srl!”

	+ Position Music, the independent music company founded by Tyler Bacon, has appointed veteran music executive Pete Robinson as GM of creative in Nashville. Robinson will report to Bacon and President Mark Chipello.

	Robinson was a founding partner of Big Deal Music, which became one of the industry’s leading independent music publishing companies before being acquired by Merck Mercuriadis’ Hipgnosis Songs in 2020. Robinson remained with the company through its transition to Hipgnosis until 2022 before founding Pete Robinson Consulting. Over the years he also held senior executive roles at RCA and Epic Records and was owner/operator of Dumbo Studios in New York.

	“We have a real vision for what we are building in Nashville, and Pete is the right person to help lead us into this next chapter,” Bacon said. “He is well equipped, both creatively and relationally, to work across Nashville’s music community as a whole, which is so important to us. He also has a strong track record of hiring great creative executives and I’m confident he will build a strong team in Nashville to support our songwriters and artists.”

	Position’s Nashville roster includes Dave Cohen, Matt Geroux (in partnership with the Core), Khalid Yassein (Wild Rivers), Zach Skelton, Maya K., Steve Solomon, Hunter Metts (JV with Interscope), and Kate Morgan.

	+ The ASCAP Foundation has named the winners of its 57th annual Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Awards for outstanding books, articles, liner notes and broadcast programs.

	“The authors, journalists, and filmmakers we honor this year illuminate the soul of music creation across concert, rock, R&B, folk, musical theatre, and children’s music, ensuring the stories of music innovators are preserved with the depth and distinction they deserve,” said The ASCAP Foundation Executive Director, Patricia Leonard.
	

	The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Broadcast/Media Award in pop music recognizes directors Isaac Gale, Ryan Olson and David McMurry for their documentary film Swamp Dogg Gets His Pool Painted, released in 2025, a unique storytelling of the legendary cult R&B musician Jerry “Swamp Dogg” Williams’s and his housemates’ musical creative life in Los Angeles surrounding his pool.

	The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Broadcast/Media Award in concert music recognizes radio host and producer Gail Wein for “Classical Gas,” produced by Classical Voice North America, the 2025 podcast series of interviews with classical musicians available on multiple platforms.

	A Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Rick Beato for his 2025 YouTube series, Everything Music, exploring music, technology and issues facing music creators in today’s industry.

	The ASCAP Foundation Paul Williams “Loved the Liner Notes” Award honors percussionist Ruth Komanoff Underwood for her personal essay for “Cheaper than Cheep,” the live box set from the 1974 concert film by Frank Zappa and The Mothers of Invention, on ZAPPA RECORDS/UMe.

	The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Awards in pop music are presented to:

	Gayle Wald for This Is Rhythm: Ella Jenkins, Children’s Music, and the Long Civil Rights Movement, the life story of “the first lady of children’s music,” published by University of Chicago Press.

	James O’Leary for The Middlebrow Musical: Between Broadway and Opera in 1940s America, an exploration of how musicals such as Oklahoma!, Beggar’s Holiday, and Street Scene embraced weighty stories in ways not seen before 1943, published by Oxford University Press.

	The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Awards in concert music go to:

	Lucy Caplan for Dreaming in Ensemble: How Black Artists Transformed American Opera, an account of Black innovation in American opera during the Harlem Renaissance, published by Harvard University Press.

	Tim Greiving for John Williams: A Composer’s Life, the first biography of one of the most important film composers of all time, published by Oxford University Press.

	Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Steven C. Smith for Hitchcock and Herrmann: The Friendship and Film Scores that Changed Cinema, published by Oxford University Press.
	

	The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award recipients for articles published in 2025 are as follows:

	The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award for an article in the pop music field goes to Ben Sisario, “The ‘Race Against Time’ to Save Music Legends’ Decaying Tapes,” on the intricate efforts to restore analog tapes with original recordings from Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan and more, published by The New York Times.

	The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award for an article in the concert music field goes to Esteban Meneses, “Revolución: Mexican Composers on the Rise,” a look at Mexican composers whose works are being performed, commissioned, and recorded by orchestras around the world, published by Symphony Magazine.

	Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Max Keller, “Does It Matter How A Cello Is Held? It’s a Centuries-Old Debate,“ published by The New York Times.

	The Virgil Thomson Award for Outstanding Music Criticism is presented to Gabriel Kahane for his article, “A Love Letter to Music Listings,” published by The Atlantic.

	Tuesday, Oct. 22

	After a five-decade career with BMI, Barbara Cane has announced that she will retire from the company at the end of this year. While she is leaving her current role as BMI’s Vice President of Worldwide Creative, Cane has agreed to serve in an advisory capacity to BMI, working directly with CEO Mike O’Neill.

	“After more than five decades, BMI is not simply where I have built my career — it is part of who I am,” Cane said. “It gave me the opportunity to grow, to discover, and, most importantly, to uncover the soul within the songwriter. Through every chapter of my journey, I have come to understand that creativity is not simply a profession; it is the heart of who songwriters are and the force that moves our industry forward. What has made this journey so meaningful is that my own values remain deeply aligned with those of BMI – to believe in creators, to nurture their gifts, and to create an environment in which their careers can flourish. After fifty years, that purpose still lives in my heart—and it is why this work has never felt simply like a career, but like a calling.”

	O’Neill added, “Barbara is one of the first people I met when I joined BMI almost 32 years ago, and her kindness, caring nature and warm welcome showed me exactly why she is so loved by so many in our industry. She has demonstrated that same care and attention time and again to the many songwriters she worked with, nurtured and supported, and it’s why her relationships in this industry have endured. While Barbara and I started out as colleagues, we’ve ended up as family, and I don’t know many who can say that about the people they work with. The beautiful thing for me is that Barbara has agreed to continue working with me as an advisor, allowing BMI and our writers to still have her insight and counsel, while also allowing her to enjoy some time away from us for the first time in fifty years.”
	

	Cane began working at BMI part-time in 1970 while she was still in high school and has dedicated her entire professional career to the company. She held numerous roles throughout her tenure, starting in BMI’s “Song Research” department and holding a number of creative roles including General Manager of the Los Angeles office as well as Vice President of Creative in New York, Los Angeles and London, directing the creative activities for BMI’s Pop, Rock and Indie teams.

	+ Electric Feel Publishing has signed songwriter and producer Naila to the company’s UK roster.

	Naila is a London-based, multilingual writer, producer and multi-instrumentalist from Barcelona who has worked with Joel Compass, H.lls, P2J, Gabzy, Moon Willis, Rimon, BenjiFlow, Mahalia, AoD, Dinos, JJ and ColeYoursTruly, among others. She has worked closely with and developed Spanish artists Violeta, Paula Cendejas, Chiara Oliver and Olivia Bay, as well as French artist Anaïs Cardot.

	“I am incredibly excited to become a part of the amazing team at Electric Feel, it’s a blessing to be surrounded by this amount of talent and skill and I cannot wait for the music and experience ahead with the EF family!” said Naila.

	+ Warner Chappell Music Nashville has struck a global publishing deal with Kentucky-reared singer-songwriter Elizabeth Nichols, known for her breakout single, “I Got a New One.” She made her Grand Ole Opry debut last November and has performed at Stagecoach, Lollapalooza, C2C and CMC festivals and has opened for Little Big Town, Jason Aldean, Russell Dickerson, and Jordan Davis.

	“I’m very excited to join Warner Chappell, where I can finally monetize my questionable taste in men. I have the best team in the world. Here’s to many more songs.”

	Katy Wolaver, SVP, A&R, Warner Chappell Music, shared: “Elizabeth is a breath of fresh air… witty, clever, and unabashed in taking authentic life experiences and turning them into irresistible lyrics and melodies. Her songs embrace a wide range of moods and emotions, from unique takes on relationships to political satire. In just a short time on the country landscape, she’s moved her career into high gear, and all of us at Warner Chappell are delighted to join her on what is sure to be an incredible ride.”
	

	+ Sony Music Publishing Nashville, in partnership with Taycan Entertainment, has signed rising songwriter and producer Jared Conrad to a worldwide publishing deal. Conrad has earned cuts with Cody Johnson, Lee Brice, Brothers Osborne, Ian Munsick, Randall King, Mitchell Tenpenny and Austin Snell, among many others. His credits also include co-writing Pentatonix and Meghan Trainor’s “Kid On Christmas” from Pentatonix’s Grammy-nominated album “Holidays Around the World.”

	+ Columbia Records has announced the expanded role of Manos Xanthogeorgis as Executive Vice President, Creative & Digital, leading a newly formed creative team while continuing to oversee digital across the labe

	In his expanded role, Xanthogeorgis will oversee creative and art direction, short- and long-form content, and the label’s digital functions, including audience development, viral marketing and social.

	“What I love about music is that something deeply personal to an artist can become just as personal to someone they’ve never met. Finding new ways to help that happen is what keeps this work so exciting for me,” said Xanthogeorgis.

title: Jenna Ortega Does Not Read Reviews, Watch Her Own Movies or Check the Box Office — and Plans to ‘Be Off TV for a While’ After ‘Wednesday’ Ends
description: Jenna Ortega opened up to Vogue magazine as part of a new cover story about her nonexistent relationship to how the public receives her movies. In
body:
Jenna Ortega opened up to Vogue magazine as part of a new cover story about her nonexistent relationship to how the public receives her movies. In other words, the “Wednesday” star does not watch her own movies or read reviews (because “that would send me into a psychosis of some sort’) or check the box office updates when her team sends them her way (because “I don’t want it to become a numbers thing”).

	For most of her movie career, Ortega would rely on social media to gauge the chatter around her projects or to find out how much word of mouth existed around a certain project. But she’s even doing less of that these days since she’s on social media “less and less” because “so much of what you see on there nowadays is just garbage AI,” plus “we all look at ourselves too much.”
	

	Ortega told Vogue that she recently broke her phone and didn’t even bother to get it fixed for a few days so she could be without social media and technology at her fingertips. She explained: “If I needed to get somewhere, if I had a workout class, I would look at a map on the computer, memorize the streets. If somebody needed me, I’m like, ‘Well, I’m gonna be at this café at this time.’ And that was so freeing.”

	Ortega is gearing up for the release of her movie, the Taika Waititi-reviewed “Klara and the Sun.” Reviews have not been kind to the movie, which is adapted from the Kazuo Ishiguro novel of the same name. Variety panned the film as “calamitous” and a “strained, whimsical comedy that’s ruinous.” The movie currently boasts a 27% on Rotten Tomatoes and is only tracking for a box office debut in the $2 million range despite a $20 million production budget. Fortunately for Ortega, she will stay clear of the reviews and the box office grosses.
	

	In a separate interview on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, Ortega got more reflective about her television career. She currently headlines Netflix’s blockbuster series “Wednesday,” which is heading into its third season on the streamer. Ortega got her start on TV when she debuted at 9 years old on “Jane the Virgin” and went on to find Disney stardom on three seasons of “Stuck in the Middle.” Whenever “Wednesday” finally comes to an end, Ortega will be taking a TV break.

	“What I’m meant to do will come and find me,” Ortega said. “I think after ‘Wednesday,’ I’ll probably be off the TV for a while. You know I had many years doing [TV]. I was bouncing from show to show as a kid and I want to leave time for new things.”

	Read Ortega’s full Vogue cover story here. “Klara and the Sun” opens in theaters Oct. 23.

            Britt McHenry was back in the sports spotlight Wednesday night ... but the former ESPN reporter wasn't calling the action, she was causing it ... throwing a drink on a fan and getting escorted out of an NBA game to a chorus of boos ... and it's all on video.
      
    
            The current U.S. State Department press advisor got into a heated confrontation at the Washington Wizards' home opener ... and we obtained video showing her tossing a beverage at someone in the crowd.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            But sources close to Britt tell TMZ there's more to the story ... claiming people sitting behind her and her male guest were making inappropriate comments about Kyle Kuzma's fiancée, Winnie Harlow ... and Britt responded. Kuzma used to play for the Wizards and now plays for the Milwaukee Bucks, their opponent in Wednesday's game.
      

            Our sources don't recall exactly what prompted Britt to throw the drink, but say it was part of the confrontation ... and claim things were thrown at her, too. They also claim the group behind them were saying inappropriate and misogynistic things to Britt to instigate her.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Folks weren't exactly rolling out the red carpet for her exit ... several people began tossing rally towels in her direction as she made her way through the stands as boos rained down.
      
    
            Britt, however, appeared unfazed by the hostile reception ... blowing kisses toward the crowd and waving on her way out ... though she was later captured on camera arguing with a security guard who was directing her to leave the building.
      
    
            Despite the exchange, sources close to Britt insist she wasn't kicked out ... telling us she left on her own to head to the bar, while her male guest stayed behind and met up with her after the game.
      
    
            The Wizards went on to defeat the Bucks, 128-116.
      
    
            Britt previously worked as an ESPN correspondent and a Fox Nation commentator before landing her current role with Trump's State Department.

title: Tom Skerritt, 'Top Gun' and 'Alien' Star, Dead at 93
description:

body:
'Top Gun' Star Tom Skerritt
                          Dead at 93

                              October 22, 2026
                            12:16 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 22, 2026
                                1:39 PM PDT
                                    
              
    
            Tom Skerritt, the veteran actor best known for his roles in "Top Gun," "Alien" and "Picket Fences," has died.
      
    
            The Emmy-winning star died Wednesday of natural causes, his family confirmed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "We are heartbroken by his loss," his family said, remembering him for his humor, wisdom and generosity.
      

            The family added ... "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Skerritt's Hollywood career spanned six decades ... kicking into high gear with his breakout role in the 1970 war comedy "M*A*S*H."
      
    
            He went on to play Captain Dallas in the 1979 sci-fi classic "Alien" and Tom Cruise's no-nonsense instructor Viper in 1986's "Top Gun."
      
    
            On the small screen, Skerritt starred as Sheriff Jimmy Brock on "Picket Fences" ... winning an Emmy for the role in 1993.
      
    
            His other credits include "Steel Magnolias," "A River Runs Through It," "Cheers" and "Ted."
      
    
        
                    
                      06/11/2009
                  
      
    
            The last time we got Skerritt out was back in 2009 at LAX when we discussed his illustrious career ... and asked if there would ever be a sequel to "Top Gun."
      
    
            Before Hollywood came calling, the Detroit native served in the U.S. Air Force ... later becoming an advocate for veterans.
      
    
            He was 93.
      
    
            RIP
